metadata.title: Evolution of the computational science community: The dynamics of topics and collaborations in 24 years of ICCS and JoCS publications

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This study does not use an ILSA micro-dataset (e.g., PISA/TIMSS/ICCS student responses) and therefore does not define a student sampling frame, school clustering, or survey-weight variables. The analysis is based on bibliographic and textual corpora: ICCS proceedings papers (LNCS and Procedia) and JoCS journal papers (ScienceDirect), after excluding corrupted files and non-research content (editorials, board updates, workshop information). Because there is no complex survey design, no sampling weights (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or replicate weights (e.g., BRR/JRR) are applicable. The only weighting-like step is within the text-mining pipeline (e.g., standardized popularity scores normalized by the number of papers per year), which is not a survey-weighting procedure.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible Values (PV) are not applicable because the dependent variables are not cognitive achievement scores from an ILSA assessment; instead, the study constructs topic/disciplines popularity scores and network measures from publication text and metadata. The paper also does not describe an ILSA-style missing-data protocol for PV-based outcomes, since the dataset is a curated corpus of publications rather than student response data. As a result, PV handling and PV-related missing-data handling are outside the scope of the study design.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study constructs two corpora: (1) ICCS proceedings papers collected from Springer LNCS (2001–2009 & 2018–2024) and Elsevier Procedia Computer Science (2010–2017), and (2) JoCS journal papers obtained from ScienceDirect (all issues 2010–2023). Pre-processing includes eliminating corrupted files due to coding issues and excluding editorial information, journal editorial-board updates, and workshop information. After pre-processing, the ICCS corpus contains 7861 papers and the JoCS corpus contains 1817 papers (Table 1). For text processing, only main paper content from abstract through conclusion & discussion is retained; appendices, references, links, and other irrelevant information are removed, and POS tagging (spaCy) is used to chunk professional terminology and abbreviations before TF-IDF vectorization.

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICCS the study leveraged the reported predictors to predict Primary study outcome (heuristic migration), finding that This paper is a bibliometric/science-of-science study rather than an ILSA-based predictive ML study: it analyzes the evolution of computational science topics and collaboration networks using ICCS proceedings (2001–2009 & 2010–2017 & 2018–2024) and JoCS journal articles (2010–2023). The authors build a discipline classification library (15 first-level disciplines, 213 second-level disciplines) and represent papers with TF-IDF vectors, then compute cosine similarity to assign discipline relevance and derive standardized popularity scores normalized per 100 papers per year. They report validation of the topic-discovery approach via Pearson correlations between topic assignments under different numbers of selected disciplines (e.g., Table 3), and they characterize network structure using scale-free distribution fits, clustering coefficients, and edge-weighted co-occurrence networks (e.g., Tables 6–8). No student-level outcomes, survey weights, PVs, or supervised ML models are trained; therefore, there are no predictive performance metrics (e.g., accuracy/RMSE) for a target variable. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.null_fields_interpretation: The extraction is sparse because the manuscript does not perform ILSA-style student-level predictive modeling. It uses publication text and metadata to compute topic popularity and network statistics, with no defined ILSA program/cycle/grade/domain, no PV-based achievement outcomes, and no supervised ML training/evaluation. Consequently, fields required for empirical ML on ILSA microdata (e.g., main_findings with target-variable prediction metrics, PV handling, missing-data handling for student responses, and survey-weight usage) are not applicable to this study’s design.
